strings.notice_title: A research tool, not medical advice
strings.notice_body:
OREVID generates hypotheses for researchers: which existing drugs might be worth studying for a disease. The candidates have not been tested in patients for that disease, many will be wrong, and some could be harmful.

Do not use them to start, stop or change any treatment. If you have questions about your own treatment, ask your doctor.

strings.candidates_help: Existing drugs ranked highest by the model, excluding those already approved here, and only if they are indicated for a disease that significantly shares associated genes with this one (≥ 3 genes, hypergeometric p < 10−5). How often they are right: when known treatments are hidden, 22-27 % of these candidates rediscover them; against new approvals unknown to the graph (the most realistic test), about 4 % (chance would be < 0.1 %). Caution: random gene sets of the same size pick candidates that are right just as often, so the shared genes are not evidence of a shared mechanism; the hit rate comes from the model's ranking and from the drug's use in related, well-studied diseases (see Method). They are hypotheses to prioritise, not predictions. Model order; click a row to see its evidence.

method:
Method and validation

Full description, statistics and limitations in the preprint (DOI 10.20944/preprints202610.1918.v2).

What it does. For each disease, it ranks ~8,000 PrimeKG drugs using paths in a knowledge graph (genes, proteins, diseases, phenotypes, side effects, interactions): e.g. «the drug acts on a gene involved in the disease» or «the drug already treats diseases that share genes with this one». A ranking model (LightGBM, LambdaRank) learns which paths matter. The order favours drugs specific to this disease over drugs that score high everywhere. The score is not a probability.

What is shown. Of the model's top 25, only those with a line of evidence we have checked actually works. Hit rate within the top 25 in retrospective validation (hidden treatments; «hard» = diseases with no near-identical relative in the graph), on the benchmark where the rule was fixed and on an independent split (9 whole disease areas hidden):

EvidenceBenchmarkBenchmark, hardAreasAreas, hardNew approvals
Indicated for a neighbouring disease in the ontology (direct extensions)50 %13 %59 %25 %12.6 %
Indicated for a disease sharing genes (≥ 3, p < 10−5, not counting genes linked to ≥ 500 diseases) (candidates)24 %28 %28 %24 %4.4 %
Neither (hidden)4 %3 %2 %2 %1.5 %

Why these two: «the drug acts on a disease gene», with nothing else, has a 2-3 % hit rate, the same as having no path at all; and sharing genes with a disease that has thousands of associated genes (p ≥ 10−5) has 0-2.5 %. So they do not count. An adverse effect matching a disease phenotype (SIDER) is shown as information, but it does not separate contraindications from indications and is not a warning. If a disease has little information in the graph, we say so instead of filling the list. The hypergeometric test draws from the 19,766 genes with at least one associated disease (corrected on 14 October 2026: diseases were also counted before, which made p-values too small; the threshold moved from 10−6 to 10−5 so that the same candidates are kept).

What the shared genes mean (and what they do not). In a permutation test, the gene set of every disease was replaced by a random set of the same size (genes drawn in proportion to how many diseases they are linked to), keeping the ranking and the drugs' indications. The candidates selected this way were right as often as those selected by the real shared genes (5.2 % against 4.4 % on new approvals), also within each range of gene-set size and when at least 3 specific genes are required. Genes associated with 500 diseases or more (about 55 genes, mostly developmental genes linked to many rare syndromes, such as FGFR3, GLI3, TP53 or COL2A1) no longer count since 23 October 2026: the candidates they alone brought were right 1–3 % of the time, like hidden ones. Against curated drug mechanisms (DrugMechDB) the shared genes do contain a protein of the real mechanism more often than random genes of the same disease (25 % against 17 % of 447 drug–disease pairs), but they do not select better drugs than random gene sets of the same size. So the shared genes are not evidence of a shared mechanism: the line works because it picks drugs already used in diseases of similar size and research intensity. We keep the rule because its hit rate is measured, but the genes on each card are context, not an explanation. Three pre-registered replacements (shared enriched Reactome pathways, specificity-weighted genes, genetic evidence only) did not beat that null on the new approvals either; pathway overlap came closest (5.0 % with half the candidates).

How to read these figures. Hiding known treatments and checking whether the model recovers them is the usual test (TxGNN's too), but it rewards rediscovering what is already known. The «New approvals» column is more realistic: indications approved according to Open Targets that are not in the graph. There, a table candidate is right roughly 1 in 20-25 times (those sharing specific genes 4.8 %, generic genes 2.8 %), roughly 60 times more than chance (about 0.07 %), and this is a lower bound (many real indications are not approved). They are hypotheses to prioritise research.

Risk warnings. We cannot predict whether a new drug would improve or worsen a disease. We only flag a warning when the drug is contraindicated in more neighbouring or similar diseases than it is indicated for, or when it blocks immune checkpoints in an autoimmune disease. Measured on already-labelled drug-disease pairs, 97 % of those flagged by the first rule are contraindications (base rate 77 %); it could not be measured on new candidates. No warning does not mean safe: the warning does not detect a mechanism opposite to approved treatments (e.g. an anticholinergic in Alzheimer disease) or a class toxicity (e.g. pneumonitis from EGFR inhibitors in pulmonary fibrosis). The safety column also shows recorded adverse effects (SIDER) that match disease phenotypes, as information.

Validation. Compared with TxGNN (Harvard, Nature Medicine 2024), run with its official code on the same PrimeKG splits, in a public, reproducible benchmark (OREVID-bench). Recall@100 = fraction of the correct drugs found in the top 100:

TestPopularityTxGNNRotatEOREVID
«New» diseases (zero-shot, 5 seeds)0.360.410.290.81
Same, without near-identical diseases0.200.260.160.54
Whole disease areas hidden (9)0.190.240.220.62
Approvals missing from PrimeKG (Open Targets)0.130.120.160.36

RotatE is a knowledge-graph embedding (PyKEEN) with its settings chosen on one seed (details); combining it with OREVID did not help. OREVID-bench figures. The web additionally orders by specificity (to avoid drugs that show up everywhere), which costs about 0.01 Recall@100 in the same tests. Two protocol differences were measured (fairer comparison): with OREVID trained only on the training labels, as TxGNN, and without the few diseases where TxGNN gives every drug the same score, the result is 0.81 against 0.42 (hard subset 0.53 against 0.28; areas 0.63 against 0.24).

Test against the future. The model was retrained on the graph as it was known at a cutoff year (2012, and 2015 as a confirmation fixed beforehand: indications and Open Targets associations that appeared later were removed) and asked to rank the uses that later reached phase 3 or approval. At 2015, Recall@100 was 0.32 against 0.17 for popularity (difference 0.15, 95 % interval 0.12–0.17; the pre-registered rule required the interval to exclude 0). Within the top 25, 5.4 % of direct extensions, 3.1 % of candidates and 0.8 % of hidden drugs later reached phase 3 or approval. Limits: 80 % of PrimeKG indications have no date and stay in the training graph, and for non-obvious uses (no close relative already indicated) the advantage is small (0.04). A model turning the section, rank and gene-set size into a calibrated probability was tested and not adopted: it improved on the section rates by only 2.5 % (rule: at least 5 %).

Limitations. The data reward rediscovering known treatments. For drugs with no prior use, no model (including this one) does well. Direction relies on recorded contraindications and may be missing for new drugs. The data contain known errors: wrong gene-disease associations at the source (e.g. subacute bacterial endocarditis carries lupus GWAS genes, which brings antibiotics up as lupus candidates), comorbidities read as shared biology, and Open Targets approvals not confirmed by any single-drug label or regulatory report (shown as «unconfirmed»; no Open Targets approval counts as evidence). Status (approved, withdrawn…) is DrugBank's, which does not always flag withdrawals. That is why every candidate shows where it comes from. It is a tool to prioritise research, not to decide treatments.

Practical information. The «Generic» column says whether a generic or biosimilar of the same active ingredient is on the market: in the US (FDA Orange Book, marketed generic applications; FDA Purple Book, licensed biosimilars) and in the EU (EMA, centrally authorised medicines only: generics authorised country by country are missing, so «no EU generic» does not mean there is none). When there is no US generic, the year the latest US patent or exclusivity ends is shown. Matching is by active-ingredient name and single-ingredient products only. The «Studied» column counts clinical trials (Open Targets, any phase) and articles that mention both the drug and the disease (PubTator3); «underexplored» means no trial and at most 2 articles. None of this changes the ranking: a drug off patent is cheaper to test, not more likely to work. Match rates and a manual check are in PRACTICAL.md.

Data. PrimeKG 2023 (aggregate; includes DrugBank, CC BY-NC 4.0, and SIDER and DisGeNET, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Open Targets Platform 26.06 (CC0; includes ChEMBL mechanisms and molecules), STRING 12.5 (CC BY 4.0), PubTator3 (public domain). Results under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, non-commercial use. Details in the legal notice.

about:
About OREVID

What it is. OREVID (Open Repurposing Evidence) is an open tool that ranks existing drugs for each disease and shows the evidence behind every candidate, together with how often that kind of evidence turned out to be right. It is meant for researchers who want to prioritise drug-repurposing hypotheses, not for decisions about patients.

Who is behind it. OREVID is an independent, non-profit project created and maintained by Joaquim Quadrada Jané, an industrial engineer with a Master's degree in Data Science (Universitat Oberta de Catalunya) and over 25 years of experience in engineering and R&D in industry (automotive, textiles and technology). He develops OREVID in a personal capacity, independently of his employer, to see how far open data and careful validation can go in helping medical research. It has no institutional affiliation, no funding and no commercial interest, and there are no conflicts of interest to declare.

Why. Many repurposing tools give a score without saying why, or report only their best-looking numbers. OREVID tries to do the opposite: every rule that decides what is shown was fixed before looking at the results and then confirmed on independent data, the realistic hit rates are published next to the optimistic ones, and anyone can rebuild everything from the public sources.

How it was built. The code was written and reviewed with the help of AI (Claude, by Anthropic). Every number on this site comes from code that is public and can be re-run; the decisions taken along the way, including the mistakes found and corrected, are recorded in the repository.

Independent checks. The comparison with TxGNN uses its official code on the same data splits, in a public benchmark (OREVID-bench), including a fairer comparison that removes the protocol differences. Independent reproductions and criticism are welcome.

Open. Code under the MIT licence, data and results under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Cite the preprint: Quadrada Jané J. OREVID: Open, Evidence-Based Drug Repurposing with a Benchmark Against TxGNN. Preprints.org, 2026. DOI 10.20944/preprints202610.1918.v2. Code and data: DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23323226.

Contact. Errors, expert opinions and collaboration proposals: contact@orevid.org or GitHub issues.
